prompt: What is the difference between a homopolymer and a copolymer?

choices.text: A homopolymer is made of identical repeating units; a copolymer forms when two or more different monomers polymerize together
A homopolymer is made by chain-growth polymerization; a copolymer is made by step-growth polymerization
choices.why: The distinction is the number of different monomers, not the method of synthesis.

choices.text: A homopolymer has no branches; a copolymer always has branches
choices.why: Only graft copolymers have branches of another monomer. Random, alternating, and block copolymers need not.

choices.text: A homopolymer is isotactic; a copolymer is atactic
choices.why: Tacticity describes stereochemistry (Section 31.2). Homopolymer and copolymer describe how many different monomers are present.

explanation: Homopolymers are made up of identical repeating units. Copolymers are obtained when two or more different monomers polymerize together, and they are more important commercially. Copolymerization often gives properties quite different from those of either homopolymer.

prompt: Saran is made by copolymerizing vinyl chloride with vinylidene chloride in a 1 : 4 ratio. How many vinylidene chloride units are used for each vinyl chloride unit?
explanation: Copolymerization of vinyl chloride with vinylidene chloride (1,1-dichloroethylene) in a 1 : 4 ratio gives Saran, so there are 4 vinylidene chloride units for every vinyl chloride unit. Table 31.3.1 lists its uses as fibers and food packaging.

prompt: SBR (styrene–butadiene rubber) is used for tires and rubber articles. Which monomers is it made from?

choices.text: Styrene and 1,3-butadiene
Acrylonitrile and 1,3-butadiene
choices.why: That pair gives nitrile rubber, used for adhesives and hoses.

choices.text: Isobutylene and isoprene
choices.why: That pair gives butyl rubber, used for inner tubes.

choices.text: Acrylonitrile, 1,3-butadiene, and styrene
choices.why: All three together give ABS, named for the monomer initials and used for pipes and high-impact applications.

explanation: Table 31.3.1 lists SBR (styrene–butadiene rubber) as a copolymer of styrene and 1,3-butadiene, used for tires and rubber articles.

prompt: Which copolymer in Table 31.3.1 is made from hexafluoropropene and vinylidene fluoride, and what is it used for?

choices.text: Viton, used for gaskets and seals
Saran, used for fibers and food packaging
choices.why: Saran is made from vinyl chloride and vinylidene chloride, not the fluorine compounds.

choices.text: Nitrile rubber, used for adhesives and hoses
choices.why: Nitrile rubber is made from acrylonitrile and 1,3-butadiene.

choices.text: Butyl rubber, used for inner tubes
choices.why: Butyl rubber is made from isobutylene and isoprene.

explanation: Table 31.3.1 lists Viton as the copolymer of hexafluoropropene and vinylidene fluoride (CH2=CF2), used for gaskets and seals.

prompt: Nitrile rubber is used for adhesives and hoses. Which monomers is it made from?

choices.text: Acrylonitrile and 1,3-butadiene
Styrene and 1,3-butadiene
choices.why: That pair gives SBR, used for tires.

choices.text: Vinyl chloride and vinylidene chloride
choices.why: That pair gives Saran.

choices.text: Isobutylene and isoprene
choices.why: That pair gives butyl rubber, used for inner tubes.

explanation: According to Table 31.3.1, nitrile rubber is a copolymer of acrylonitrile (cyanoethene) and 1,3-butadiene; the name comes from the nitrile (–C≡N) group of acrylonitrile.

prompt: Butyl rubber, a copolymer of isobutylene and isoprene, is used for what, according to Table 31.3.1?

choices.text: Inner tubes
Food packaging
choices.why: Food packaging is a use of Saran.

choices.text: Gaskets and seals
choices.why: Gaskets and seals are uses of Viton.

choices.text: Adhesives and hoses
choices.why: Adhesives and hoses are uses of nitrile rubber.

explanation: Table 31.3.1 lists butyl rubber, made from isobutylene (2-methylpropene) and isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene), for inner tubes.

prompt: ABS is named for the initials of its monomers. How many different monomers are copolymerized to make it?
explanation: ABS is made from three monomers: acrylonitrile, 1,3-butadiene, and styrene. Table 31.3.1 lists it for pipes and high-impact applications.

prompt: When monomer A is copolymerized with monomer B, what decides the exact distribution of A and B units in the chain?

choices.text: The initial proportions of the two monomers and their relative reactivities
Only the temperature of the reaction
choices.why: The section names two factors: the initial proportions of the monomers and their relative reactivities.

choices.text: Whether the polymer is later heated above its glass transition temperature
choices.why: Heating a finished polymer doesn't rearrange the monomer units in its chain.

choices.text: The molecular weight of the finished polymer
choices.why: Molecular weight doesn't decide the order of units. Initial proportions and relative reactivities do.

explanation: A copolymer of A and B might have a random or an alternating distribution of the two units. The exact distribution depends on the initial proportions of the two reactant monomers and their relative reactivities.

prompt: What does the section say about the monomer distribution in most real copolymers?

choices.text: Neither perfectly random nor perfectly alternating copolymers are usually found; most have many random imperfections
Most copolymers are perfectly alternating
choices.why: In practice, perfectly alternating copolymers are not usually found.

choices.text: Most copolymers are perfectly random
choices.why: In practice, perfectly random copolymers are not usually found either.

choices.text: Most copolymers are block copolymers
choices.why: Block copolymers are prepared only under certain conditions. Most copolymers have many random imperfections.

explanation: The exact distribution of monomer units depends on the initial proportions and reactivities of the monomers. In practice, neither perfectly random nor perfectly alternating copolymers are usually found; most copolymers have many random imperfections.

prompt: A copolymer chain has the sequence –A–A–A–A–A–B–B–B–B–B–A–A–A–A–A–, with long runs of each monomer. What type of copolymer is this?

choices.text: A block copolymer
A graft copolymer
choices.why: In a graft copolymer, branches of one monomer hang off a main chain of the other. Here all units are in one chain.

choices.text: An alternating copolymer
choices.why: An alternating copolymer would read –A–B–A–B–, switching every unit.

choices.text: A random copolymer
choices.why: In a random copolymer A and B units are scattered without pattern, not gathered into long runs.

explanation: Block copolymers are those in which different blocks of identical monomer units alternate with each other, as in long runs of A followed by long runs of B. Graft copolymers have homopolymer branches of one monomer grafted onto a homopolymer chain of another.

choices.text: A homopolymer chain of one monomer with homopolymer branches of another monomer attached
A chain in which blocks of identical units of each monomer alternate
choices.why: That is a block copolymer.

choices.text: A chain in which the two monomer units alternate one by one
choices.why: That is an alternating copolymer.

choices.text: A chain in which the two monomer units are scattered without pattern
choices.why: That is a random copolymer.

explanation: Graft copolymers are those in which homopolymer branches of one monomer unit are "grafted" onto a homopolymer chain of another monomer unit, like chains of B branching off a stem of A.

choices.text: Polymerization of one monomer is started, then an excess of the second monomer is added to the still-active reaction mix
A finished homopolymer is gamma-irradiated in the presence of the second monomer
choices.why: That is how graft copolymers are made.

choices.text: Both monomers are mixed in a 1 : 1 ratio before the reaction starts
choices.why: Mixing both from the start gives a random or alternating distribution, not blocks.

choices.text: Two finished homopolymers are melted and pressed together
choices.why: The section describes adding the second monomer to the still-active chains of the first.

explanation: Block copolymers are prepared by initiating the polymerization of one monomer as if growing a homopolymer chain and then adding an excess of the second monomer to the still-active reaction mix, so a block of the second monomer grows onto the first.

prompt: Graft copolymers are made by gamma irradiation of a completed homopolymer chain in the presence of a second monomer. What does the irradiation do?

choices.text: It knocks hydrogen atoms off the chain at random points, creating radical sites that start polymerization of the second monomer
It breaks the chain into individual monomers that then recombine with the second monomer
choices.why: The homopolymer chain stays intact and becomes the stem; branches grow from radical sites on it.

choices.text: It adds a proton to the chain, creating carbocations that start cationic polymerization
choices.why: Gamma irradiation removes hydrogen atoms, generating radicals, not carbocations.

choices.text: It removes all the double bonds from the second monomer
choices.why: The second monomer must keep its double bonds to polymerize onto the new radical sites.

explanation: In graft copolymer synthesis, high-energy gamma irradiation knocks hydrogen atoms off the homopolymer chain at random points, generating new radical sites that initiate polymerization of the added monomer. The new chains grow as branches from the original chain.

prompt: In an alternating segment of butyl rubber, each repeat unit is one isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) unit joined to one isobutylene (2-methylpropene) unit. How many carbon atoms does one such repeat unit contain?
explanation: Isoprene, H2C=C(CH3)CH=CH2, has 5 carbons and isobutylene, (CH3)2C=CH2, has 4. Polymerization adds monomers without losing atoms, so one alternating repeat unit, –CH2–C(CH3)=CH–CH2–CH2–C(CH3)2–, has 5 + 4 = 9 carbons (Exercise 31.3.1).

prompt: Irradiating poly(1,3-butadiene) and then adding styrene gives a graft copolymer used for rubber shoe soles. What is the structure of this copolymer?

choices.text: A polybutadiene main chain with polystyrene branches
A polystyrene main chain with polybutadiene branches
choices.why: The irradiated homopolymer, poly(1,3-butadiene), becomes the main chain; the added styrene grows as branches.

choices.text: Alternating styrene and butadiene units in a single chain
choices.why: That would be an alternating copolymer. Grafting gives branches of one homopolymer on a chain of the other.

choices.text: A long block of polybutadiene followed by a long block of polystyrene
choices.why: That would be a block copolymer, made by adding the second monomer to still-active chains, not by irradiation.

explanation: Gamma irradiation of a completed homopolymer creates radical sites along its chain, and the added monomer polymerizes from those sites. Irradiating poly(1,3-butadiene) and adding styrene therefore gives polystyrene branches grafted onto a polybutadiene chain (Exercise 31.3.2).
